steps.caption: A relief map uses different colours to show the altitude of the land above sea level. Mainland Spain has a large plateau, mountain ranges and depressions.

photo.alt: Relief map of mainland Spain with the Meseta, the mountain ranges and the depressions coloured by altitude

steps.caption: The Meseta is the large central plateau of mainland Spain. The Sistema Central divides it into two parts: the Submeseta Norte and the Submeseta Sur.
Some mountain ranges are in the Meseta, some surround it and others are beyond it.
The Montes de Toledo are a mountain range in the Meseta.

photo.alt: Montes de Toledo: a mountain range in the Meseta, with rounded slopes above green scrubland

steps.caption: The Cordillera Cantábrica is one of the mountain ranges surrounding the Meseta.

photo.alt: Cordillera Cantábrica: a high, rocky mountain above green slopes

steps.caption: The Pirineos are a mountain range beyond the Meseta. Aneto (3,404 m) is their highest peak.

photo.alt: Pirineos: high, pointed rocky peaks above a mountain lake

steps.caption: Depressions are areas of land lower than the land around them. Mainland Spain has two large depressions: the Depresión del Ebro and the Depresión del Guadalquivir.
The Depresión del Ebro is a large area of land lower than the land around it.

photo.alt: Depresión del Ebro: low land with the river Ebro between fields and pale cliffs

steps.caption: Mulhacén (3,478 m), in the Sistemas Béticos, is the highest peak on the mainland. Aneto (3,404 m) is in the Pirineos. Teide (3,718 m), in the Islas Canarias, is the highest mountain in Spain.

questions.explanation: There are 2 large depressions: the Depresión del Ebro and the Depresión del Guadalquivir.

questions.prompt: Which mountain range is Mulhacén, the highest peak on the mainland, in?

questions.prompt: Why is Mulhacén the highest peak on the mainland but not the highest mountain in Spain?

Because Mulhacén is in the Meseta
Because Mulhacén is in the Islas Baleares

questions.prompt: The Sistema Central divides the Meseta. Which are the two parts?
questions.explanation: The Sistema Central divides the Meseta into the Submeseta Norte and the Submeseta Sur.

steps.caption: An archipelago is a group of islands. Spain has two main archipelagos: the Islas Canarias, in the Atlantic Ocean, and the Islas Baleares, in the Mediterranean Sea.
The Islas Canarias are in the Atlantic Ocean. They have eight main islands of volcanic origin: they were formed by volcanoes.

photo.alt: Relief map of the Islas Canarias: La Graciosa, Lanzarote, Fuerteventura, Gran Canaria, Tenerife, La Gomera, El Hierro and La Palma

steps.caption: La Graciosa, Lanzarote and Fuerteventura are flatter. The other islands are higher and steeper.
Teide, on Tenerife, is a volcano. At 3,718 m, it is the highest mountain in Spain.
The Islas Baleares are in the Mediterranean Sea. They are an extension of the Sistemas Béticos.

photo.alt: Relief map of the Islas Baleares: Mallorca, Menorca, Ibiza, Formentera and Cabrera

steps.caption: The Islas Baleares have five islands. Mallorca is the largest. The other islands are flatter than Mallorca.
Mallorca has varied relief: the Sierra de Tramuntana and the Pla, a plain in the centre of the island. Its highest peak is Puig Major (1,436 m).

branches.label: Pla
items: A plain in the centre of the island

steps.caption: The coast is the land next to the sea. Spain has an extensive and varied coastline surrounded by the Atlantic Ocean, the Cantabrian Sea and the Mediterranean Sea, so it has three coasts: Cantabrian, Atlantic and Mediterranean. The Cantabrian coast is generally rocky, with high cliffs and small inlets, such as at Cabo de Ajo.

photo.alt: Map of the coasts of Spain with their capes, gulfs, rías and deltas

steps.caption: Atlantic coast: the coast of Galicia is irregular, with many long inlets called rías, such as the Ría de Arousa. Cabo Fisterra is also on this coast.

photo.alt: Ría de Cedeira, A Coruña: a long inlet of the sea between green hills

steps.caption: Atlantic coast: the coast of Atlantic Andalucía, on the Golfo de Cádiz, is low and sandy, with marshes near the coast.

photo.alt: Playa de Matalascañas, Huelva: a low, sandy beach at sunset

steps.caption: Atlantic coast: the coast of the Islas Canarias is high and rocky in the western islands and much lower in the eastern islands.

photo.alt: Acantilados de Los Gigantes, Tenerife: very high cliffs above the sea

steps.caption: Mediterranean coast: Cataluña and the Illes Balears have high rocky areas and low sandy areas with small coves. Cabo de Creus, the Golfo de Roses and the Delta del Ebro are on the coast of Cataluña.

photo.alt: Cala Llombards, Mallorca: a small cove with a sandy beach between rocks

steps.caption: Mediterranean coast: the Comunitat Valenciana and the Región de Murcia have wide beaches, as along the Golfo de Valencia.

photo.alt: Altea, Alicante: a wide beach on the Mediterranean coast

steps.caption: Mediterranean coast: Mediterranean Andalucía has beaches and cliffs. Playa de Mónsul is near Cabo de Gata.

photo.alt: Playa de Mónsul, Almería: a beach between rocks and cliffs

photo.alt: Playa del Chorrillo, Ceuta: a low beach next to the town

photo.alt: Cliffs on the coast of Melilla, high and rocky above the sea

steps.caption: Spain's rivers are very different. Some are long and others are short. Some have an abundant flow all year and others have a very low flow in summer. The flow is the amount of water that a river carries.
There are no true rivers in the Islas Canarias and the Islas Baleares. The archipelagos have gullies and torrents that only carry water when it rains.

tiles.label: No true rivers on the islands

steps.caption: Rivers flow into the Mediterranean Sea, the Atlantic Ocean and the Cantabrian Sea, so Spain has three basins. A basin is an area of land where all the rivers flow into the same sea or ocean.
Mediterranean basin: the Ebro is long, with an abundant flow. Other rivers, such as the Júcar, the Segura and the Turia, are short, with a low flow, and they are almost dry in summer.
The Júcar flows into the Mediterranean Sea. It is short, with a low flow, and it is almost dry in summer.

photo.alt: Júcar: a river between hills in the Mediterranean basin

steps.caption: Atlantic basin: the rivers in Galicia, such as the Miño, are short, with an abundant flow. Others, such as the Duero, the Tajo, the Guadiana and the Guadalquivir, are long, with a lower flow in summer.
The Tajo flows into the Atlantic Ocean. It is a long river, with a lower flow in summer.

photo.alt: Tajo: a long river in the Atlantic basin, winding between wooded hills

steps.caption: Cantabrian basin: rivers such as the Nalón and the Narcea are short because they start near the coast. They have an abundant flow because it rains frequently all year round.

chain.label: Start in mountains near the coast

steps.caption: The Narcea flows into the Cantabrian Sea. It is short, with an abundant flow, because it rains frequently all year round.

photo.alt: Narcea: a short river in the Cantabrian basin, flowing through a green valley

steps.caption: Climate and relief change rivers. Rivers through areas of high precipitation have an abundant flow; rivers through dry areas have a low flow and can become dry in summer. Rivers that start in mountains near the sea are short; rivers that start a long way from the sea are long.

tiles.label: Start far from the sea → long

questions.prompt: The Ebro reaches the sea at the Delta del Ebro. Which coast is the Delta del Ebro on?
questions.explanation: The Delta del Ebro is on the Mediterranean coast, in Cataluña.

steps.caption: Human activities can damage landscapes. So the authorities create protected areas in places of high ecological value.
The authorities recover damaged areas by removing waste, planting trees and removing pollutants from the water. They prevent harmful activities with studies of their impact on the environment.

tiles.label: Studies of the impact on the environment

steps.caption: There are different types of protected areas. A national park has the highest level of protection.
Spain has 16 national parks. They represent mountains, wetlands, Mediterranean forests, the landscapes of the Islas Canarias and marine areas.

Spain's 16 national parks, part 1: Picos de Europa, Islas Atlánticas de Galicia, Ordesa y Monte Perdido, Aigüestortes i Estany de Sant Maurici, Sierra de Guadarrama, Monfragüe, Cabañeros and Tablas de Daimiel.

tiles.label: Aigüestortes i Estany de Sant Maurici

steps.caption: Spain's 16 national parks, part 2: Doñana, Sierra Nevada, Sierra de las Nieves, Archipiélago de Cabrera, Caldera de Taburiente, Garajonay, Teide and Timanfaya.
Wetlands are flat areas covered by salt or fresh water, permanently or temporarily. They include lagoons, deltas, marshes and lakes, such as the Tablas de Daimiel, the Delta del Ebro and Doñana.
The Tablas de Daimiel, in Ciudad Real, are a wetland protected as the Parque Nacional de las Tablas de Daimiel.

photo.alt: Tablas de Daimiel, Ciudad Real: a wetland with shallow water, reeds and a wooden walkway

steps.caption: The Delta del Ebro, in Tarragona, is a delta: a wetland where the river Ebro meets the Mediterranean Sea.

photo.alt: Delta del Ebro, Tarragona: a flat delta wetland with birds flying over the water at sunset

steps.caption: Wetlands are home to a great variety of animals and plants. They are stopover points for European birds migrating to Africa, and they help combat climate change by capturing carbon and reducing atmospheric greenhouse gases.

tiles.label: Stopover for birds migrating to Africa
Capture carbon and reduce greenhouse gases

steps.caption: More than half of the wetlands have disappeared or suffer from overexploitation of groundwater, water pollution caused by fertilisers and pesticides, and the expansion of human settlements. They are protected by restrictions on water extraction, hunting or fishing, and some are protected areas, such as the Parque Nacional de las Tablas de Daimiel.

tiles.label: Restrictions on water extraction, hunting or fishing
